HERE’S HOW YOU ... can now do 
a better life-saving job ... by using 

THE STEPHENSON “MINUTEMAN” 



RESUSCITATOR — It Is Really Three Machines In One: 

1. RESUSCITATOR — for use when the accident victim is 
not breathing. Due to drowning, smoke, suffocation, drug poison, 
electric shock, war gas, hemmorhage, stroke, severe heart failure 
and the like. 

2. INHALATOR — for use when he can breathe but needs 
more oxygen. This is true when the patient needs more than the 
20% oxygen contained in ordinary air. A steady stream of oxygen 
is delivered into the mask where the patient can breathe it. 

3. ASPIRATOR — for use when mucus, froth (usually present 
in drowning cases) or blood clogs his air passages. It provides 
suction for removing this material from the throat into a bottle 
so that oxygen can reach the lungs.

Canadian Camping 







Cditox ^ Preamble 


It is one thing to experience a busy 
year; nearly everyone can make that 
statement and be truthful about it. 
But it is something else again to be 
extremely happy about that busy-ness, 
it having been created by a group of 
co-operative, self-less people: the 
readers of this magazine, members of 
the editorial committee, and members 
of the Canadian Camping Association 
who come forward so freely with ideas, 
with articles, with tangible help and a 
tremendous amount of encouragement. 
It is easy to carry on under such 
pleasant circumstances, and to say with 
all sincerity: “We thank you very 
much, and look forward to an even 
busier year in the fall, if it means more 
members and a stronger, more closely- 
knit Association”. 

We have arrived at many conclusions 
during the past season; notably, that 
new members are easy to find. Camp 
directors and other individuals inter¬ 
ested in the camping movement are 
ready and eager to join our ranks, to 
share our experiences and knowledge; 
they are waiting to hear from us. By 
the same token, we feel that next 
year’s membership numbers could be 
doubled if we knuckle down to the 
actual business of the project. 

We have learned that Canadian 
Camp Week is tremendously important 
to Canada as well as to the Associa¬ 
tion. It is important nationally because 
it has to do with youth, its develop¬ 
ment, adjustment and general well¬ 
being. It is important to the Associa¬ 
tion because it gives us a chance to 
tell our story, to place ourselves before 


the citizens of Canada, and to increase 
our stature, our prestige, in the eyes 
of members and general public alike. 

This year was a first attempt on our 
part, true enough. A very efficient 
committee has worked to put Camp 
Week across, but we have had to learn 
as we progressed. And the astonishing 
outcome is that enthusiasm rides high 
with the public, provincial Associations, 
and key people in all districts. They 
are ready to hear about us and to help 
in an extensive public relations pro¬ 
gramme. Department stores in major 
centres in Canada responded this year 
with interior and window displays. J. 
Frank Willis of CBC gave us full sup¬ 
port, with the result that John Fisher, 
Cuckoo Clock House, TV Tabloid, a 
series of spot announcements from such 
centres as Montreal, Ottawa, Toronto 
and western points did a tremendous 
amount to put our story across. Edi¬ 
tors of daily and weekly newspapers 
responded valiantly as well. 

With these results at hand, it is 
obvious that CCA is missing a tremen¬ 
dous opportunity, not only for campers, 
but for counsellors and directors, if we 
fail to make Canadian Camp Week the 
giant yearly event it should be. We 
should, therefore, see that a strong 
standing committee is appointed espec- 
cially for this project, to begin work 
now for 1955 all across the board. 

We have learned that campers and 
camp directors would welcome a song 
book produced by the Canadian Camp¬ 
ing Association. Each province has its 
own peculiar camp songs along with 


Toronto , CanadaJune , 1954 


7 



the old favourites known to campers 
the world over; each camp has its own 
versions of old songs, as well as original 
arrangements. All these and more, we 
want to know about. If every camp 
director in our membership would sub¬ 
mit even one original song or original 
verses to an old one, Mrs. Dorothy 
Douglas, our Song Book Chairman, 
would be well away to a completed 
venture. Let’s not say “something 
must be done about the Song Book 
this summer”; rather let us all, today, 
set down, clip, beg, or borrow the 
words and music she needs, and mail 
them NOW. 

Any claim to fame this magazine 
may possess is due to all those fine 
people who write for us, like DR. H. 
W. CURRAN, who so generously 
presented us with his address “to be 
used at will” in Canadian Camping 
. . . ARNOLD FRASER, whose close 
association with “Ace” made him the 
obvious author of this month’s Per¬ 
sonality . . . BARRY LOWES, busy 
as any other camp director at this time 
of year, a first-line man in the Ontario 
Seminar for Camp Directors, yet who 
made time to help us and cheer us on 
rainy days . . . KEITH CLEVERDON, 
who also pushed aside the hours to 


write on a subject none likes to face 
but must, Fire Protection . . . MARY 
PORTER, enthusiastic Queen’s student, 
and student OCA member whose con¬ 
cern for waterfront safety caused her to 
work out, with the help of Don Purdy 
of the Ottawa Red Cross, a rescue 
system for waterfront emergencies . . . 
KIRK WIPPER wasn’t exactly un¬ 
busy when he produced an excellent 
waterfront check-list all camp directors 
will keep for future reference wc are 
sure. 

As we go to press, we extend con¬ 
gratulations and best wishes for a very 
successful future to Mr. Irwin Halad- 
ncr and his new CCA Executive, as 
well as to the newly-elected Quebec 
Camping Association Executive, names 
of which appear in this issue of the 
magazine. 

So . . . wherever we pitch camp this 
summer, from Queen Charlotte Island 
to the Grand Banks, may we all be 
blessed with happy, sunny days. 

Please excuse us while we fold our 
tent with the typewriter in it and 
silently steal away . . . yes, to camp, 
too . . . before the office telephone 
dares to ring once more!

Canadian Gamiung 



WE WENT TO KINGSTON 



The LaSalle Hotel in Kingston saw 
one of the best Annual Meetings we 
have ever had, and the laurels go to 
President Ted Yard for carrying it 
through so efficiently. More than a 
few comments on his efficient handling 
of the event reached our ears, and the 
entire gathering showed pleasure and 
satisfaction at the progress in all 
provinces, and in the value of friendly 
discussion and positive suggestion for 
our next steps forward. 

Although the representatives (from 
Montreal, Ottawa, Kingston and Tor¬ 
onto) were not large in number, we 
were strong in determination to 
broaden membership, to strengthen ties 
between provinces, to gain through 
Camp Week wider recognition across 
our country, and to make this the 
beginning of a new era in Canadian 
camping. 

That we have come a long way in 
the last three hundred and sixty-five 
days is only too evident in the Presi¬ 
dent’s resume of accomplishments: 

Preparation of book on Policies and 
Procedures, 

Setting up of Camp Week Com¬ 
mittee, 

Discussion with lawyer re charter, 

Special binding of Camping Maga- 
zines, 

Invitation to Canadian Council of 
Churches to have a representative 
on our Board, ; v 

Reduction of amount of fees received 
from provinces. 


Development of special membership 
promotion material, 

On-going correspondence of the 
committee, 

Setting up of new Song Book Com¬ 
mittee, 

Extensive distribution of free pam¬ 
phlets and other material to inter¬ 
ested people, to camping associa¬ 
tions across Canada. 

After the work of the nominations 
committee, the following executive was 
elected: Honorary President, Mr. A. L. 
Cochrane; President, Mr. Irwin Halad- 
ner, formerly Vice-president of CCA, 
past-President of OCA and present 
treasurer of OCA; Vice-presidents, 
Mrs. J. H. McDonald, Winnipeg; Mr. 
F. M. Van Wagner, Montreal; Mr. 
Charles Roche, Vancouver. 

Facing us is another busy year of 
progress, headed by the new Executive. 
In his address of welcome, Mr. Yard 
pointed up the extremely valuable con¬ 
tributions to the Association as a whole 
given by Mr. A. L. Cochrane, and by 
Mr. Irwin Haladner. He stressed too 
the importance of including members 
from other provinces who, as we have 
already seen through Mrs. McDonald 
and Mr. Van Wagner, can bring the 
viewpoint of other parts of Canada 
into the discussions. By the time the 
magazine is in your hands, Mr. Halad¬ 
ner will have called his first Board 
meeting, and new committee chairmen 
will have been appointed.

Education for Conservation 

Taken from the address presented at the Annual Meeting of 
The Canadian Camping Association, Kingston, by 

Dr. H. W. Curran, Professor of Biology, Queen's University 


Conservation practices and methods 
have improved more in the last twenty 
years than in all previous history. 
Though this increase has been tremen¬ 
dous both in application as well as in 
appreciation of conservation, there is 
still room for improvement. But I am 
encouraged to believe that this interest 
will continue to develop when we con¬ 
sider the number of persons and agen¬ 
cies now concerned in Conservation. 

First I should define some of the 
terms. Here, I am referring to the 
Conservation of our natural renewable 
resources, primarily our forests, our 
trees, our grass and other plant life; 
our wildlife, which includes all our wild 
mammals, our birds, both game birds 
and songbirds; our fishes, both game 
fish and commercial fish; and some¬ 
times even the amphibians and reptiles. 
Our resources include as well, water 
and soil which should be carefully con¬ 
trolled. Conservation has often been 
defined as the greatest use, by the 
largest number of people over the 
longest period of time. More briefly it 
can be described as “Wise Use”. If 
then, we accept the wise use of our 
natural renewable resources for the 
term Conservation, we can examine 
some of the developments and present 
practices. 

Since the beginning of the 20th 
century, there has been a steadily 
increasing interest and appreciation of 
the conservation of our natural re¬ 
sources. This got under way very 
slowly at first and was initiated by 


such militant campaigners as W. T. 
Hornaday, who crusaded with mission¬ 
ary zeal to bring to the attention of 
the general public their rapidly dimin¬ 
ishing natural resources. Many Cana¬ 
dians and Americans obtained their 
first interest in nature through the 
late Jack Miner, who did so much to 
arouse public interest in Wildlife Con¬ 
servation. 

The famous Theodore Roosevelt, 
President of the United States, and 
Gifford Pinchot, Governor of Pennsyl¬ 
vania, helped to set aside vast tracts of 
land as forest reserves. But with the 
advent of the First World War there 
was a decline in interest in conserva¬ 
tion by the public. This brought about 
a consequent decline in fish and wild¬ 
life resources. The picture was indeed 
a dark one and it appeared certain 
that many species were going down 
a fading trail to extinction. Little was 
accomplished during this period and 
through the 20’s, with the outstanding 
exceptions of the Migration Bird 
Treaty Act—which was the first Inter¬ 
national Treaty to protect Migratory 
Birds—and the great and good work 
of the Audubon Society and the Junior 
Audubon Bird Clubs, which had an 
effect later on as these children grew 
to adults. 

It was during the 30’s that there 
was the greatest increase in conserva¬ 
tion interest and activities, which has 
gradually built up and culminated in 
a peak which has never been reached 
before. This present peak of attain- 


10 


Canadian Camping 



ment could not have been dreamed of 
by those pioneer conservationists in the 
early part of the 20th century. 

In general, there was a great increase 
as well along the following lines:— 

1. Protective regulations. 

2. Stocking and Planting of fish and 
game. 

3. Reforestation. 

4. Improvement of environment, 
both aquatic and terrestrial. 

After the end of the Second World 
War there was a tremendous expan¬ 
sion in the Fish and Game Depart¬ 
ments and Conservation Commissions 
and Agencies. There is still a serious 
shortage of trained personnel in the 
Fish and Wildlife Field. 

With proper management, it has 
been possible for some kinds of game 


and fish to make astonishing recoveries. 
To consider a few examples, the great 
American Bison herds on the Western 
plains were reduced from more than 
thirty million animals to only twenty- 
one individuals in less than forty years. 
Now they have been brought back to 
all that the regions will support in a 
wild state, several thousands; also the 
American Pronghorn Antelope of the 
western plains was nearing extinction; 
now it is once more common. 

The beaver, symbolic of Canada, and 
the most important animal in our 
country’s history, was exterminated 
over most of its range. By careful 
management, live trapping and release 
into new areas, it is now re-established 
over much of its original range.

Canada's Leading 
CRUISERS 


SAILBOATS 


on the Western Channel 


TORONTO 


Toronto , Canada, June, 1954 


11 






The white-tailed deer is now prob¬ 
ably more common in many places in 
the States than when the colonists 
first arrived. One reason is that it can 
do much better in second growth or 
scrub area than in heavy forests. It 
is necessary to have hunting seasons 
for such animals to reduce their 
numbers over the winter or many will 
die of starvation. 

All of these cases and many more 
are possible through proper wildlife 
management to provide sufficient food 
and shelter. Adequate management is 
essential to meet the greatly increased 
demands upon our resources. 

In most areas where counts have 
been made, it has been shown that the 
number of sportsmen has at least 
doubled in the past ten years. Also, 
that most of these persons are spending 
twice the amount of time in the field. 
Thus, in angling at least, we find in 
many places that man-hours of fishing 
has increased by four hundred per cent 
within ten years, because twice the 
number of fishermen are spending twice 
the amount of time fishing. 

Another startling example close to 
home indicates the increase among 
hunters in Ontario. The number of 
resident deer licenses sold in Ontario 
in 1933 was approximately seventeen 
thousand, and in 1943 it was thirty- 
eight thousand, but ten years later, in 
1953, it had risen to seventy-eight 
thousand. We can expect no lessening 
of these figures, but probably an in¬ 
crease. 

These are only indications of a 
trend for use of the great out-of-doors. 
These figures are for anglers and 
hunters, but that is only a small per¬ 
centage of the total numbers that enjoy 
our lakes and woods. This army of 
tourists, of campers, canoeists and 
hikers can not be accurately tabulated, 


but we know that it is increasing year 
by year and that the average amount 
of time spent by each individual is 
also increasing. 

It is these people, making up an 
increasingly large proportion of the 
general public, that are bringing about 
such profound changes in the attitude 
towards conservation, and especially 
the young people and children. 

Education for Conservation should 
reach to all levels of society and to 
all ages of the population, but it is 
most effective with the young people 
and school children. 

Undoubtedly the best method for 
true appreciation of our natural re¬ 
sources and the proper use of them is 
by education. Not only the education 
of adults through such organizations 
as Naturalists Clubs, Fish and Game 
Clubs, Home and School Groups, 
Audubon Societies, and others, but 
especially through the young people 
in our elementary and secondary 
schools. This is where it is most effec¬ 
tive and where within a very few years, 
results will begin to show. 

Conservation teaching should be 
embodied in part of the program of 
our schools today—not as an additional 
subject in an already overloaded cur¬ 
riculum, but as an approach or a 
philosophy in such fields of study as 
History, Geography, English, Social 
Studies and others. Of course it is an 
integral part of Biology and Agricul¬ 
tural Science. 

Conservation should not imply the 
prohibition of the use of our resources, 
whether forests, fish or wildlife. Let us 
consider instead that Conservation is 
the wise use of our resources. 

Let us hope that Canadians, through 
education and appreciation, will be 
able to use and enjoy their resources 
wisely and well.

Canadian Camping 


AMONG OURSELVES . . 

c4lnold 3\a£er, Executive Secretary , 

High Park YMCA, Toronto. 


To those of you who do not know 
him, I would like to introduce you to 
"‘Ace 5 ’ Milks, official initials W. A., the 
man whose life and work have been 
devoted to Camping and who has made 
more impact on Institutional Camping 
in Canada than any other. There will 
be few indeed who do not know Ace, 
and for them this will be no introduc¬ 
tion, but rather a calling to mind of 
that pleasant, warm personality who 
carries in his heart a love of people and 
‘n his whole being a basic understand¬ 
ing of a man’s relationship to nature 
and to God. 

For 34 years, Ace directed Camp 
On-Da-Da-Waks, one of the largest 
Y.M.C.A. camps in Canada and one 
of the most progressive. The Ottawa 
Y.M.C.A. owes a great debt to Ace for 
the years of service he gave to the 
development of this splendid camp, 
and thousands of men and boys in the 
capitol and indeed all over the con¬ 
tinent still look back to those happy 
days spent at Camp On-Da-Da-Waks 
and their association with him. 

Ace Milks was born in Eardley, 
Quebec, and as early as 1907 attended 
the Ottawa Y.M.C.A. Camp at Mar¬ 
shall’s Bay on the Ottawa River. This 
was not the first camp which the 
Ottawa Y.M.C.A. had organized for 
boys and, as a matter of fact, the 
origin of Y.M.C.A. camping in Ot¬ 
tawa is somewhat lost in the mists of 
history. The first actual word of the 
camp, which was to become Camp 
On-Da-Da-Waks, is to be fonnd in the 
minutes of an Ottawa Y.W.C.A. Board 
meeting. It states that a camp had 
been held in 1893 on the Ottawa River 


across from Quyon, Quebec. However, 
Ace was with Wallace Forgie in 1908, 
when the camp was first moved to 
Golden Lake, Ontario, because there 
was too much sawdust in the water 
at Marshall’s Bay. It was in the year 
1915 that Ace assumed the role of 
leadership at Golden Lake, becoming 
a camp counsellor and subsequently 
in 1916 he became Assistant Director 
of the camp of which Charlie Plewman 
was Director. Every summer from 1916 
to 1950 inclusive, Ace directed Camp 
On-Da-Da-Waks, a total of 34 years. 

Ace’s original interest in camping 
was based on his love of the out-of- 
doors, the swish of the paddle, the

(continued from page 13) 

enjoyment of the things of nature, 
coupled with his love of people and 
his reverence for the Creator. Thirty- 
four years have seen a lot of changes 
in the field of camping. Not only did 
Ace keep abreast of these changes, but 
through his splendid work and the 
development of his own camp, he 
caused many of these changes to take 
place. One of his strong points has 
always been his ability to interest the 
community in the best type of camp¬ 
ing and to surround himself with the 
best type of laymen who have supported 
Camp On-Da-Da-Waks through whose 
ability, together with Ace’s guiding 
genius, have maintained Camp On-Da- 
Da-Waks in its first-rank position 
among Y.M.C.A. Boys’ Camps in 
Canada. Developments in camping, as 
in anything else, have always depended 
on the committed support of laymen 
who are prepared to give time and 
effort, and Ace knew how to recruit 
these men and to release their abilities 
in a productive manner. As Ace’s 34 
years in camping went by, he helped 
to shape the philosophy of not only 
Y.M.C.A. Camping, but organizational 
camping in general and to this day he 
is still the spirit of youth with a keen 
interest in the movement. As a layman, 
he continues to give the best of his 
guidance and experience to camping 
in Ottawa. He believes that a camp 
experience is vital to every boy and 
girl, is an important part of education. 
His undying love of nature reminds one 
of Rousseau. Perhaps it is this love 
of nature that led him to pick the name 
On-Da-Da-Waks, which means “Men 
of the Woods”, for the camp at 
Golden Lake. 

In 1950, the year in which Ace 
retired, Camp On-Da-Da-Waks served 
over three hundred boys and possessed 
a most modem plant and equipment, 
with which to do the job. Under his 


direction over the years, the camp made 
the most of its site, increased its prop¬ 
erty holding and prepared itself to 
continue to serve the youth of the 
future. Through Ace’s leadership, 
Camp On-Da-Da-Waks has always pro¬ 
vided an opportunity for boys to meet 
outstanding Canadian artists, natural¬ 
ists and leaders. Because of his early 
contact with Wallace Forgie, the boys 
of Camp On-Da-Da-Waks have always 
taken an interest in lands outside 
Canada and have supported those who 
are less fortunate. The leadership 
which Ace Milks has given to many 
thousands has not been narrow or 
confined, but has been as broad as 
the wide blue skies under which he 
has loved to work. 

Ace Milks has never confined his 
interests to his own camp at Golden 
Lake alone. He has given the benefit 
of his experience, in an advisory 
capacity, to many camps across Canada, 
and has personally helped to start 
Christie Lake Boys’ Camp, Woodland 
Camp and Shirley Bay Camp. He still 
serves on these camp committees, be¬ 
lieving that boys, no matter from what 
walk of life they come, should have 
the benefit of a camping experience. 

We who have been in camping and 
who know its values, are aware of its 
great impact on the development of a 
philosophy of life. As much as any 
man I know, Ace Milks represents that 
way of life. Organizational camping 
at its present high level of development 
owes much to the vision and the per¬ 
sistent effort which Ace Milks has 
brought to his own Camp On-Da-Da- 
Waks and to the movement as a whole. 
I hope the day will come when we 
recognize service such as he has 
rendered, for we build on what he 
started, based on the philosophy of 
deep understanding of nature and of 
people. 


Toronto , Canada , June , 1954

PROVINCIAL REPORTS 


BRITISH COLUMBIA 

Membership 1953-54 

Camps 18, Agencies 3, Individuals 23, 
Students 20. 

Camp Counsellors’ Institute 

A very successful Institute for Coun¬ 
sellors and administrators was con¬ 
ducted on May 1 and 2. Approxi¬ 
mately 50 counsellors and 33 admin¬ 
istrators attended the sessions. Dis¬ 
cussion leaders were Mr. and Mrs. 
Larry Handy, Geneal Secretary, Y.M. 
C.A., Wenatchee. 

B.C. Camping Week, 1953 

For the second consecutive year, this 
week was geared to bringing the values 
in camping to the attention of the 
public. Promotion consisted of several 
daily press articles, radio talk and spot 
plugs, four city store window displays, 
two outdoor illuminated message signs, 
and talks to parent groups. Of great 
assistance were posters given by the 
A.C.A. and overprinted by us for local 
use. 

Programme 

Monthly general meetings have not 
been successful for several years in 
RC. This is partly due to the high 
ratio of agency camps, whose directors 
and staff are tied up all year in their 
other programmes and cannot devote 
time to meetings. Commencing last 
October, discussion groups in counsel- 
lorship and administration have met 
monthly with great success. Short 
announcements only were injected 
into these meetings. It is hoped to 
publish a summary of these discussions 
later. 


Highlight of the fall programme was 
the visit of National President, Ted 
Yard. Mr. Yard spent one evening 
with the executive and the following 
week spoke at the monthly general 
meeting. We are indebted to Mr. Yard 
for his visit and the inspiring message 
he brought, not only to our Associa¬ 
tion, but also to the other groups he 
spoke to, including the University 
Physical Education Department. It is 
the hope of the Association that such 
a visit will be made by each President 
at some time during his/her two year 
period of office. 

Programme Material 

Commencing at the Institute last 
May, programme material has been 
sent to the membership at regular 
intervals and has met with enthusiastic 
approval. Stencils of the material have 
also been sent to the National Office 
and others will be sent if requested. It 
is planned to continue the distribution 
of this material. 

Camp Directory 

1953 saw the first printed camp 
directory, published in conjunction 
with the Community Chest & Council. 
Negotiations are under way to publish 
the 1954 directory. 

Buyers’ Guide 

Vice-President Mrs. Pat Broome has 
been working hard to compile material 
and information that will assist camp 
directors and/or managers in the’r 
buying of camp supplies. This has 
been a big job, but we feel sure that 
the results will justify the amount of 
work involved.

Health Cards 

A standard Camper’s Health Report 
Card is the aim of the Provincial 
Department of Health. With this in 
mind, the Department approached this 
Association for their help and guid¬ 
ance. Following two meetings with the 
executive, a satisfactory card was 
drawn up with the endorsation of this 
Association. These cards will be dis¬ 
tributed free of cost through the 
licensing branch and all camps are 
being requested to make use of them. 

Pacific Camping Federation 

The annual conference of the above 
Federation is being held at Harrison 
Hot Springs Hotel, B.C., on March 
10-11-12. A delegation from this Asso¬ 
ciation will be attending and their 
report will be published in the March 
issue of the Newsletter. Negotiations 
are also under way to arrange an 
affiliation with the Pacific Camping 
Federation. 

1954 Canadian Camp Week 

Under the chairmanship of Mrs. 
Carola Forst, the committee is busy 
lining up sources of publicity for this 
week, which promises to be a big 
event this year. Already Vancouver’s 
three department stores (Eaton’s, 
Woodwards, HBC) have promised one 
window each for display purposes.

Alberta Camping Association report 
of the meeting held on February 13th, 
1954. 

Present were the following: Mr. Joe 
Currie, Pioneer Ranch Camp; Murray 
Faulkner, Y.M.C.A., Calgary; Mrs. 
Watson, Provincial C.G.I.T. Board; 
Jean Angus, R.E.C.A. Council, Harold 


Robbins, Chairman Lethbridge Y.M.- 
C.A. Camp Committee; a representa¬ 
tive of Kiwanis Camp; Jean Martin 
and Kay Broatch, representing Y.W.- 
C.A. and the Council of Social Agen¬ 
cies; Jim Scott and another representa¬ 
tive from the Provincial Boy Scouts 
and Girl Guides Associations; Mr. 
Cooney, representing Camp Katakasu 
and the Provincial Red Cross Swim¬ 
ming and Water Safety Board. 

Minutes of the previous meeting 
were read and approved and new¬ 
comers were introduced. Murray 
Faulkner then presented the proposed 
constitution for the Alberta Camping 
Association which was then discussed 
at some length and revisions in the 
wording and structure were suggested. 

Moved by Jim Scott and seconded 
by Jean Martin that the constitution 
be adopted as revised at this meeting, 
also the executive as elected at the 
previous meeting be now definitely 
appointd to carry on for the first year 
of operation, with the addition of Jean 
Martin, Calgary Y.W.C.A., as Treas¬ 
urer. Carried. 

The Executive is as follows: 

Murray Faulkner, President; Harold 
Sprague, Vice-president in charge of 
Program; Chester Robbins, Vice-presi¬ 
dent in charge of Memership; George 
Hilton, Secretary; Jean Martin, Treas¬ 
urer. 

Chester Robbins presented a mem¬ 
bership report: To date we have 10 
applications for membership in the 
Alberta Camping Association and fur¬ 
ther applications have been sent out 
to all parties that we think will be 
interested in this type of venture. 

Membership in the Alberta Camping 
Association is to be on three levels: 

(1) Camps or organizations, (2) Group 


Toronto, Canada, June, 1954 


17 



membership, (3) Individual member¬ 
ship. 

Certain recommendations were then 
made to the program committee from 
the general meeting rgarding a pro¬ 
posed Alberta Camping Conference to 
be held the first week of May in 
Edmonton. This conference to coin¬ 
cide, if possible, with Canadian Camp¬ 
ing Week. 

It was announced at this meeting 
that Harold Sprague of Edmonton had 
been appointed as Alberta representa¬ 
tive to the Nominating Committee of 
the Canadian Camping Association. 

In conclusion, it now stands on the 
records that the Alberta Camping 
Association has been formally organ¬ 
ized, its executive elected for this year 
of 1954 and great hopes are held for 
its future in the Alberta Camping 
field. 


MANITOBA 

An “Ideal” is never totally achieved, 
although certain of its goals can be 
accomplished in part at least. So it 
has been with the Manitoba Camping 
Association in the past year. 

Some of the subjects contained in the 
eight meetngs held by the Association 
in 1953 were, a study of Staff Training 
for Camps, the “History of Camping 
in Manitoba”, presented at the Open 
Meeting, the report from the Associa¬ 
tion’s delegate to the Ontario Camp¬ 
ing Association Conference, a panel on 
Camp Programs, the Camping Con¬ 
ference, the Fall meeting with Mr. 
Yard, and lastly, this Annual Meeting. 
This was a varied program, planned 
to meet as many of the interests ex¬ 
pressed by the members as possible 
and highlighted by the two stimulating 
visits of the President of the Canadian 
Camping Association, Mr. Ted Yard.

Into the meetings, planning and pro¬ 
grams of the Association went the hard 
work of many of the members serving 
on panels, Committees, etc. More 
publicity was done to acquaint the 
Community with the fact that they 
have a Camping Association; the Camp 
Directory was published, and Campers 
across Canada were made more aware 
of the Manitoba Section through repre¬ 
sentation at the Ontario Conference, 
and as a result of Mr. Yard’s visits. 

Although it can be seen that the 
Camping Association has moved for¬

still far from becoming real. The goals 
as set out in the constitution have been 
touched on, in part only. The whole 
area of Community understanding and 
support has just begun. These and 
other goals are attainable and provide 


a stimulating and interesting challenge 
for the Manitoba Camping Association 
in 1954.

tunity of thanking you, and in particu¬

At times we have felt the need for 
more gatherings of kindred spirits, and 
with this in mind we arranged a few 
informal gatherings of those interested 
in private camps, where their own 
special programmes and problems were 
discussed. These meetings were held 
in addition to the regular meetings of 
the Association. 

Rgular meetings held during the 
year were open to all members, and 
as mentioned above, we had a few 
special meetings for camp directors. 
Perhaps our most successful meeting 
was held with Miss Mary Edgar as our 
guest speaker. She gave us a very 
stimulating address and we were sorry 
when it was all over. It seems at times 
that we can’t hear enough from an 
outstanding speaker. There isn’t 
enough time. 

Our Conference was held on March 
27, 28, 1953, with Bob Rourke as the 
opening speaker. Other Conference 
leaders were Irwin Haladner, Ron 
Perry, Dr. H. Caplan, John Venters, 
Walter Meyer, Dr. A. MacLeod, Roy 
Locke, Nathan Markus. About three 
hundred people attended the various 
sessions of the Conference. 

Everything considered, we believe we 
have passed a successful year. Plans for 
the coming season also show a strong 
likelihood of a good year ahead. A 
very strong slate of officers has been 
arranged by the nominating committee. 
The Annual Meeting will be held on 
May 7th in the form of an abbreviated 
conference. We open at 4:00 p.m. for 
registration. Dr. Taylor Statten will 
speak at 5:00 p.m. on “The Camper, 
What is She/He Like?” This is a 
repeat of his New York address. This 
will be followed by a dinner. Dr. Mary 
Winspear will be the speaker. The 
Annual Meeting will be held while 
some of the younger members of the 
group will have an evening of square 
dancing.

Canadian Camping 



Those ?!?! Rainy Days 

Barry G. Lowes, 

Director , Camp New Moon 


Do you dread rainy days at camp 
or do you take them in your stride? 
No matter how deeply you bury your 
head in the dry sand, wishing and 
hoping, it is still going to rain at some 
time during the summer, maybe even 
for days on end. 

If rain follows a week of hot active 
days, then a sleep-in and a late break¬ 
fast can do wonders towards recharg¬ 
ing everyone‘s “battery”. Or how 
about breakfast in bed served by the 
staff? Campers love it. (Don’t over¬ 
use it.) That’s fine for the first day, 
but what if the rain doesn’t stop? 

The most important thing is . . . 
don’t be caught unprepared. 

During your pre-camp training 
period and throughout the summer, 
conduct recreational evenings for the 
staff, centering around different active 
and quiet games that can be used later 
with their own groups on rainy days. 
Have counsellors conduct the games 
and contribute their favourites. Not 
only are they fun but they are a 
wonderful source of ideas also. 

Make a survey of your facilities. 
What buildings, what rooms, what 
space can be used on rainy days? For 
what could each be used? How many 
will each hold? Considering your own 
limitations, make out a list of rainy 
day programme possibilities, both in¬ 
door and outdoor, active and quiet. 

Set up a file index of rainy day 
activities, centrally located for quick 


references, or mimeograph copies of 
possible activities for distribution to 
the staff. 

Constantly add books of proven 
worth to your reference library. 

Insure that every counsellor has 
enough activity ideas at his fingertips 
to carry him through two rainy days. 

Instead of rainy days being days off 
for specialty counsellors, why not form 
them into committees to work with 
campers on unit or camp-wide rainy 
day programmes ? 

How about injecting specialty coun¬ 
sellors into cabins to relieve cabin 
counsellors for a while during these 
demanding days? 

Yes, be prepared, but don’t impose 
your programme. Before you empty 
your own bag of tricks, draw out 
ideas from the campers and involve 
th^m in the planning and execution 
of the program. They will probably 
surprise you. However, if this source 
runs dry, here are a few suggestions 
to help brighten the long days. 

QUIET PROGRAMMES 

Who doesn’t respond to A STORY 
told beside a crackling fireplace? If 
you can’t tell a story well . . . read it. 

Have campers RELATE TRIPS 
they have taken. 

Tell a PROGRESSIVE STORY. 
The leader begins the tale. When he 


Toronto , Canada, June , 1954 


21 



stops, the person on his right continues 
and so on around the group. 

PAPER BAG DRAMATICS. Each 
cabin group brings a paper bag into 
which they have put several objects. 
The bags are shuffled and each cabin 
selects one; after which they are given 
10 to 15 minutes to prepare a skit, 
making use of every article in their 
bag. Skits are then presented in turn 
to the rest of the camp. 

CHARADES. Who hasn’t enjoyed 
the hilarity of this game! Use teams 
involving everyone. You can use two, 
three, even four teams at once. One 
team acts while the others try to 
guess. 

PUPPETS. Make hand puppets 
from vegetables, balls or construction 
paper. Produce a show for the camp. 

TALENT NIGHT — MUSICAL 
NIGHT — RHYTHM BAND. 

QUIZ SHOWS — on water safety, 
campcraft or etiquette. 

A MOCK TRIAL. Set up a court¬ 
room, judge, lawyers, jury and execu¬ 
tioner. Various people are tried for 
humorous, fictitious crimes. They are 
always guilty and some hilarious pun¬ 
ishment is meted out on the spot. 


MASQUERADES. Spend the after¬ 
noon preparing. Everyone comes 
dressed as a bird, animal, historical 
person, comic strip character, movie 
star, or perhaps wears a crazy hat or 
makes a mask from a paper bag. 

WHO AM I? Pin the name of some 
person real or fictitious on each per¬ 
son’s back. Players try to find out who 
they are by asking questions of every¬ 
one they encounter as they move about. 
Answers may be only yes or no. 

How about WHAT’S MY LINE? 
— 20 QUESTIONS? — SPELLING 
BEE? Conduct sessions on CAMP- 
CRAFT, FIRST AID and WATER 
SAFETY. 

Run TOURNAMENTS in Check¬ 
ers, chess, dominoes, scrabble, table 
tennis, pick-up-sticks. 

HUMAN X’s and O’s. Set out 9 
chairs in 3 rows of 3 chairs each. Use 
two teams of any number. The chairs 
are the squares and the players from 
each team in turn sit in the chairs 
instead of marking X’s and O’s on 
paper. No coaching and it can be a lot 
of fun. 

BULL SESSIONS or informal dis¬ 
cussions in groups on any timely topic. 

Tell RIDDLES - PUZZLES. 


BOAT ACCESSORIES 

for every type of 
Water Craft

SAILS - HARDWARE - ROPE - CANVAS - PAINTS - VARNISHES 

TOM TAYLOR LIMITED

Canadian Camping 



SUNSHINE PREDICTION POOL. 
Write down your guess as to when the 
sun will first shine again. 

CONTEST. Write down as many 
campers and counsellors as you can 
name from memory. 

DETECTION. Set out a number 
of common items. Blindfold contest¬ 
ants who must guess the substances 
by their smell, taste or feel. 

ALPINE BOTTLE GARDEN. Into 
a sealer bottle put a layer of charcoal, 
pebbles, sand. Lay out a garden of 
twigs, moss, etc., on the sand. Water 
the garden, screw on the lid. Water 
will condense and rain on the garden, 
lasting for days. 

MOSS GARDEN. In a pie plate 
make a miniature garden of moss, 
twigs, toadstools, pebbles, etc. 

Don’t overlook LETTER WRIT¬ 
ING, STRAIGHTENING ONE’S BE¬ 
LONGINGS, working on INDIVID¬ 
UAL CRAFTS or GROUP PRO¬ 
JECTS. 

There is no substitute for curling 
up with a GOOD BOOK. 

ACTIVE PROGRAMS 

There is a great store of pent up 
energy that must and will be spent. 


SEEK AND FIND. Hide a number 
of objects about a large room. Teams 
try to find the objects. When some¬ 
one sees one on the list, he does not 
touch it or give away its Jocation, but 
reports to his captain. The first team 
to find everything wins. 

BARNYARD CANDY HUNT. 
Hide many candies about the room. 
Each team represents an animal, e.g. 
cow, dog, horse, duck, etc. When a 
player spots a candy, he does not touch 
it but makes sounds mimicking the 
animal he represents. The captain 
comes and claims the candy. (Very 
noisy but fun.) 

MUSICAL CHAIRS. Plus the 
variation of having people sit in the 
chairs. When the music stops, the 
moving players sit in their laps. 

MUSICAL PARTNERS. Partners 
walk clockwise in a double circle. On 
the first command the inside line turns 
around and walks counter clockwise. 
When the music stops, players must 
find their partners, join hands and 
squat. 

SIMON SAYS. Players obey any 
command given by the leader that is 
preceded by “Simon Says”. Anyone 
who obeys a command not preceded 
by the words “Simon says”, drops out.

As players improve, speed up the com¬ 
mands. 

COMBATIVES. Don’t forget In¬ 
dian hand and leg wrestles, badger 
pulls, cock fights, wrist presses, tug-o- 
wars. 

RELAYS. Even in confined spaces, 
just modify the locomotion to hopping, 
skipping, walking, etc. 

FOLK AND SQUARE DANCING, 
plus musical games. 

BLOW BALL. Two teams on either 
side of a tennis table. Players try to 
blow the ball off the opposite side. 
This can be played as an individual 
elimination game. The player who lets 
the ball get by him and lets it fall off 
the table, drops out. 

ROUND-THE-TABLE. Any num¬ 
ber of players line up around a tennis 
table. One player serves, places the 


bat on the table and moves out of the 
way around the table counter clock¬ 
wise. The receiver returns the ball, 
places the bat down and also moves 
on. The next players pick up the bats 
immediately and so play continues until 
someone commits a fault. Three faults 
eliminate a player. The last two 
remaining players must put the bat 
down and turn around in place 
between each bat at the ball. (A 
perennial favourite.) 

TUMBLING and WRESTLING on 
old mattresses. 

INDOOR GOLF. Set out 9 or 18 
holes. A hole might be a box, cup, 
pan, tin, etc. Bean or sand bags are 
tossed from hole to hole by players 
as they move about the course. Set up 
hazards. 

CARNIVAL. Set up games of skill 
and chance. E.G. tossing pennies into

a saucer floating in a- pail of water; 
drop clothes pegs into a milk bottle; 
bounce ping pong balls into a tin or 
egg carton; toss tennis balls into a

games yourself. 

INDOOR TRACK MEET. Shot 
put is a ping pong ball; discus is a 
cardboard plate; javelin is a straw; 
standing broad jump; high jump—from 
a standing position, jump as high as 
you can and make a mark on the wall 
with a piece of chalk; races are walk¬

OUTDOOR ACTIVITIES 

Unless even the ducks are hiding, 
there are some activities that can be 
conducted successfully in the rain. 
However, remember: dress properly— 
ponchos, rubber boots, hats, etc. After¬ 
wards get out of wet clothes immedi¬ 
ately, get warm before a fire and have 
a hot drink. 


HIKING. Somehow the sense of 
adventure is heightened in campers 
when they hike in the rain. Be alert, 
there is much to observe that is not 
present on dry days. 

CAMP CRAFT. How about trying 
out that waterproof lean-to? Can you 
light a fire in the rain? Demonstrate 
the reason for ditches around a tent, 
etc. 

BEACH COMBING. For drift- 
woodwood, different stones, fossils, 
plant and animal life. 

TREASURE HUNTS or SCAV¬ 
ENGER HUNTS. 

These are but a few ideas that have 
worked for us, offered in the hope that 
your rainy days at camp may be happy 
and memorable ones.

So me Thoughts 

on Tamp Fire Safety 

R. K. Cleverdon, 

Director, Camp Kandalore 


We are making steady progress in 
Canadian camping in raising our 
standards of health, safety and leader¬ 
ship. So far we have done little to 
set a standard for the protection ol 
our campers, our staff and our camps 
against damage or destruction from 
fire. The following thoughts are 
offered as a first step in making pro¬ 
gress in this important area of camp 
standards. It may well be that many 
readers will disagree with these sug¬ 
gestions, and if so, their comments are 
most welcome. Some areas may have 
been overlooked, and here too, sug¬ 
gestions are invited. 

Camp Location ... no camp should 
be located in a dead-end area in the 
forest, from which escape in case ol 
forest fire will be impossible. 

... at least two different routes 
for access and escape from the camp¬ 
site should be provided, so that person¬ 
nel may be evacuated if necessary, and 
so that firefighters can get in easily. 

. . . there should be a supply of 
water available from a lake, river, 
reservoir, storage tank, or swimming 
pool, to fight fires. 

. . . for camps located in isolated 
areas or where there is a danger of a 
bushfire surrounding the campsite, a 
plan for evacuation should be worked 
out in advance, and tested. Govern¬ 
ment personnel may be able to fight a 
fire once it has broken out, but it is 
dangerous to expect them to evacuate 
campers too. 


Buildings . . . frame camp buildings 
should be kept at least 20 feet, and 
preferably 40 feet, from any other 
frame building, except minor storage 
buildings. This will help prevent fires 
from spreading. 

. . . roofs on buildings should be 
flameproof, or of a type known as “first 
class” by fire underwriters. 

. . . overcrowding of frame buildings 
is very dangerous and leads to tragedy 
in the case of fire. A figure of at least 
30 sq. ft. per person for sleeping 
quarters, and 10 sq. ft. for dining and 
assembly halls is recommended. 

. . . two-storey frame buildings 

present special problems which must 
be understood. Fire authorities agree 
that the use of two-storey frame build¬ 
ings with sleeping quarters on the 
second floor in camps is undesirable. 
If this is necessary, then outside fire 
escapes of steel or well-braced wood 
must be provided, and the area at the 
base of the fire-escape kept free of 
weeds or other inflammable debris. 
Two-storey main buildings in which 
the second storey is a dining hall or 
assembly room are not recommended, 
since a fire may break out in a small 
room on the bottom floor and before 
it is detected, place all the occupants 
of the second floor in great danger. 

. . . dining and assembly halls should 
have at least two different exits, both 
opening directly to the outside, of 
reasonable width (36 to 44 in. per 
door rrcommended), the doors swing- 
(continued on page 28 )

(continued from page 26) 

ing out, and opening onto the ground 
level or not more than two feet above 
the ground. Where this is impossible 
due to the building’s location above the 
grade, the door must open onto a wide 
landing or ramp not less in width than 
the door. 

. . . cook stoves should not be placed 
near wood trim, should have fire- 
resistant floors below them, and ! should 
discharge into masonry chimneys, or 
into smoke pipes adequately protected 
from the surrounding frame wall by 
a metal sleeve or similar device. How 
often we read about a frame building 
burning to the ground in a few min¬ 
utes, caused by an “overheated stove”! 
So often the fire has been traced back 
to the smoke pipe going through the 
wall. Wherever possible, masonry 
chimneys should be used, and they 
must be cleaned frequently. 

. . . chimneys should have spark- 
arresting devices when the camp is 
located in a forest area. 

. . . electrical wiring must be done 
by a competent electrician according 
to standard practice, and precautions 
taken to avoid overloading any circut. 
Using heavier fuse plugs than that for 
which the circuit is designed is just 
courting disaster. 

. . . doors from camp hospitals 
should be at least 48 inches wide to 
allow moving a bed patient in his bed. 

. large sleeping tents should be 
flameproofed if gasoline or coal oil 
lanterns are used, and should be kept 
a reasonable distance apart. 

. . the same care should be given 
to space heaters as to kitchen stoves. 
If installing oil or propane heaters, be 
sure to get expert advice on the fire 
safety aspects. 

. . . flammable liquids like gasoline, 
coal oil and paint should be stored in 
a special building well removed from 


the others and locked against un¬ 
authorized entry. Remember, most fire 
insurance policies only allow ope gallon 
of gasoline to be stored in an insured 
building. 

Fire Precautions . . . the camp should 
consider having at least some of the 
standard fire extinguishers available at 
each building. 

. . . fire extinguishers include fire 
pails of water, fire pails of sand, fire 
barrels of water with empty pails near¬ 
by, soda-acid inverting-type cylinders, 
carbon tetrachloride, GO-two and 
foamite. CO-two is recommended for 
use in kitchens for grease and oil fires, 
and for fires in electrical equipment. 
Remember—don’t use water or soda- 
acid extinguishers on oil or electrical 
fires! Foamite is good but messy and 
will ruin any food with which it comes 
in contact. 

... it is recommended that fire pails 
or 5-gallon tank pumps be placed near 
each group of buildings or tents, and 
that a CO-two or alternative ex¬ 
tinguisher be placed in any danger area 
like the kitchen, pumphouse, main¬ 
tenance workshop, craft shop, or near 
the electrical generator if one is pres¬ 
ent. 

. . . consideration should be given 
to leaving off hydrants from the camp 
water system at strategic points, with 
coiled hose nearby. A pressure of 40 
lb. with 1 J /2 in. hose is advised, but 
even a smaller system is better than 
nothing. If this is not possible, a 
portable gasoline fire pump with hose 
is a good investment in peace of mind! 

. . . fire hazards like brush piles, dead 
leaves, debris or flammable waste, or 
leaves in roof valleys, should be 
destroyed. These are particularly 
dangerous if near buildings or tents, 
since a spark or a match dropped in 
a brush pile might start a fire which 
could sweep through a whole section 


28 


Canadian Camping 



of a camp before being brought under 
control. 

. . . lanterns should be well-cared- 
for, and filled by competent people. 
Surprising as it may seem, in one 
season a G.I.T. and the wife of a 
senior staff member were found filling 
coal-oil lanterns with naphtha gasoline! 
Neither knew there was any difference! 

... it is against the law to set out 
brush fires in the fire districts of 
some provinces from April 1 to October 
30 without a permit. The practice of 
setting off fireworks should be con¬ 
sidered in the same light. 

. . . extreme care must be taken of 
camp fires, council fires, and fires built 
during campcraft instruction or on 
hikes and outtrips. Everyone in the 
camp must know the proper pre¬ 
cautions to be taken. The assistance of 
the local Forestry Department in bring¬ 
ing this lesson to the camp members 
should be sought. . 

. . . garbage and other flammable 
waste which must be burned in the 
camp area should be burned in a 
proper incinerator, equipped with a 
spark arresting device, with the ground 
cleared around it, and fitted with a 
masonry or metal firebox into which 
the ashes will drop. 


Camp Fire Policy . . . and we don’t 
mean an insurance policy, though we 
presume you have one! No, the camp 
director must give serious thought to 
the whole problem of setting up a 
policy governing fire precautions, pre¬ 
vention and procedure, if one breaks 
out. 

... a responsible senior member of 
the staff should conduct a fire study 
of the camp, make recommendations 
which are acted upon by the manage¬ 
ment, and draw up a fire prevention 
program. 

.there should be a fire drill once 

in each camp period. 

• . . . campers and staff should be 
trained in putting out fires, and this 
should be practised with cookout and 
campfires. 

. . . there should be a routine inspec¬ 
tion at frequent intervals of all fire 
hazards like stoves and chimneys, wir¬ 
ing, fireplaces, brush piles and the like. 

... a procedure in case of fire should 
be worked out in advance so that 
everyone isn’t running around like the 
proverbial chicken if a fire does break 
out. 

. . . and finally, it takes but a little 
time to make the staff and campers 
“fire conscious”—and it may save a 
life!

Meeting W ateriront Emergencies 

Mary M. Porter, Formerly Waterfront Director y 
YWCA Camp Davern, Ottawa 


Sometimes I shudder to think what 
would happen if a real emergency 
occurred at some camps, those where 
waterfronts are spread out, those where 
the Intermediate and Senior rafts are 
separated by sand bars and distances 
up to six hundred yards. In such 
cases the swimming areas are not 
definitely marked, which makes close 
supervision extremely difficult. 

Most camps use the Buddy System, 
plus foam plastic devices or a variety 
of similar techniques to prevent water¬ 
front accidents. But perhaps we have 
over-empasized prevention and forgot¬ 
ten about cure. 

What would you do if a boat cap¬ 
sized ? What would you do if you 
missed one swimmer after the Buddy 
Whistle had been called? How would 
you organize a search or rescue? 

The time of the accident is too late. 
Some sort of “search system” should 
be planned in advance, ready to put 
into action in the event of such an 
emergency. Last summer as Water¬ 
front Director, the writer helped in¬ 
augurate such a system at the YWCA 
Camp Davern, with the help of Mr. 
Don Purdy of the Ottawa Red Cross 
Society. If our searchers, within four 
minutes pf the first signal, located the 
“dummy” which had been planted in 
the water, we considered it a successful 
drill. Up to that time there is a 
reasonable chance that the victim can 
be resuscitated. Every second counts.. 

Such a drill requires detailed plan¬ 
ning, a distinctive signal, speed, calm 


and quiet on the part of all who par¬ 
ticipate. The system should be out¬ 
lined to all staff in the pre-camp train¬ 
ing period, assisted by a small-scale 
demonstration. Each counsellor should 
know her particular duties, the general 
alarm signal, and the location of all 
emergency equipment. 

The signal must be distinctive, not 
easily confused with any other camp 
signals. Often a fog-horn, followed by 
a series of whistle blasts, is adequate. 
On hearing the signal, everyone in 
camp goes immediately to the water¬ 
front, WALKING, and calling 
“Drowning”. 

EXCEPTIONS: 

(a) leave one person at a fire or 
stove; keep water boiling and 
hot drinks ready. 

(b) leave those near to the Dim’.ng 
Hall (perhaps those in the office 
or craftshop). The first staff 
person in this group organizes 
the group: sends three for the 
nurse, stretchers and blankets; 
phones the doctor herself, sends 
everyone else to the waterfront. 

As everybody reaches the water, they 
tak off their shoes and heavy clothing, 
line up according to swimming ability 
and be QUIET. Two staff are 
appointed to supervise the Shallow 
Water Search. Each leader takes a 
line of the lesser advanced swimmers, 
who join hands and stand close to¬ 
gether, one line at each side of the area. 
Slowly, the lines will wade forward in 
wave formation into the centre, look¬ 
ing for the body (or “dummy” in 


30 


Canadian Camping 



(continued on next page) 
the training period) and feeling for it 
with feet and legs. Turn and repeat. 

When the body is found, the searcher 
tells the nearest counsellor and stands 
still to mark the spot. The camper 
does NOT try to rescue the body her¬ 
self. The counsellor makes the rescue 
after telling the Waterfront Director 
so that the water can be cleared of all 
searchers. 

In deeper water and the more ad¬ 
vanced swimming areas, a different 
method is required. Here a line of 
advanced swimmers and counsellors 
will line up close together and do 
successive surface dives, going from 
shallow to deep water in their own 
lanes. Again, when the body is found, 
notify the nearest waterfront counsellor 
and stay there to mark the spot. If 
the body is not found, turn and repeat. 
All those who are not needed in the 
first search should stay lined up on the 
beach to relieve tired searchers when 
necessary. In the deep water it is 
necessary that the first surface dive 
start right at the edge of the area, by 
jumping up and going down, not wast¬ 
ing the space of the three breast 
strokes. Non-swimmers are kept 
QUIET and well back on the beach 
by staff' who do not swim. 

Two or three staff are appointed to 
take the life-boat and the grappling 
irons and search beyond the deep 
water swimming area, rowing back 
and forth in a wave formation, in case 
the body has drifted out of the 
enclosed areas. 

All Waterfront Staff keep their posi¬ 
tions and watch the searchers: to dis¬ 
cover if any are tired or if anyone 
finds the body. If this is found, the 
nearest staff' makes the rescue and all 
searchers are signalled out of the water 
by a series of long whistle blasts. The 
body is brought up on the dock where 
as many as are fully qualified in 
Artificial Respiration take their turn. 



Timing should be less than four min¬ 
utes from the first whistle to the com¬ 
mencement of resuscitation. 

Several points are very important: 

Organize a drill as closely as possible 
to the beginning of each camp. An 
accident won’t wait until after you 
have had your drill. 

In four-week camps a second drill 
is a good reminder, and smartens up 
slack ways. 

Warn the staff before each drill, so 
that the Doctor will be called in only 
in cases of real emergency. No need 
to Cry Wolf unnecessarily. 

Be sure, when testing campers at the 
opening of camp, that they can do a 
surface dive. 

Impress on campers the need for 
silence to lessen confusion. Stress the 
seriousness of the whole situation, and 
that speed is absolutely necessary, that 
they take their part in the water 
regardless of what they are wearing, 
that there is no need to run for a 
bathing cap when a life is at stake. 

All boats will come to shore, away 
from the swimming area if possible. 
Their crews will join the ranks of 
rescuers. 

After the practice, take attendance 
by cabin groups. Tell the campers the 
(continued on next page) 


Toronto, Canada, June, 1954 


31 



LIMITED 


TRADE-MARK 


timing, and have any comments on the 
efficiency or lack of it given by staff 
in charge. Have them make sug¬ 
gestions for improvements for next 
time. 

Remember, the campers are curious. 
Show them the grappling irons; it 
helps to impress the seriousness of the 
situation on them. Remind the chil¬ 
dren that the practice is just a drill, 
like fire drill at school, so that they 
will not be frightened into writing 
letters home about drownings. Com¬ 
mend the group if the drill or search 
is executed efficiently; be sure to en¬ 
courage pride in a job well done. 

Each camp will undoubtedly require 
its own variations to suit local needs. 
But don’t wait until an accident occurs 
before you think how to organize a 
search or rescue. Every second counts. 
Give your prevention plan the con¬ 
fidence that comes from knowing what 
you would do in case of a Real 
Emergency.

How Hoes Your 

Waterfront Rate? 

Kirk A. W. Wipper, 

Director, Ontario Camp Leadership Centre, 

Bark Lake, Intario 


The check list below cannot be considered an exhaustive one, but it is 
one which I believe to be pertinent to the interests of the well established 
camp that has a waterfront program. Of course, some items will not apply 
to one or the other type of camp, but in any case, wherever people are associated 
with activities relevant to waterfronts, the vast majority of pointed questions 
below should be significant. 

There will perhaps be a few who will treat this “check list” lightly and 
say to themselves, But we have never had a serious water accident at our 
camp ! Statistics, however, tell us quite a different story! Almost every year 
some ^ camp somewhere has a serious accident which may be recorded as a 
“first”. Although, in most cases, blame may not be attached to the camp 
administration, yet somehow there must be a way for us to improve our camp 
to a point, even beyond the remotest accident possibility level. Let us see then 
“How does your Waterfront Rate?” 

Planning the New Waterfront 

Yes No Are you certain that you have clean fresh water? 

Is the bottom of the area firm, sandy and gradual in slope? 

Have you a stretch of sandy beach or grassy verge leading up to 
the water? 

Are there dangerous cliffs close to your waterfront? 

Is the water usually calm? 

Have you checked with local residents about ice conditions and 
what it might do to a permanent docking system? 

Have you enquired about water level changes during the summer? 
Is the prospective waterfront area free from excessive wind, dangerous 
currents, undertow or tides? 

Have you checked to make sure that at no time are domestic 
animals permitted to wade in or near your prospective water¬ 
front area? 

The Established Waterfront Area 

Yes No Have you arranged to have your waterfront carefully checked for 
newly acquired hazards, such as roots, stumps, deadheads, etc.? 
Have you arranged to clear away any new accumulation of weeds? 
Have you made plans to remove a movable rock that has previously 
not had attention due to lack of time? 

Have you checked the planking on your docks? 

Have you inspected movable parts, such as hinges, diving board 
fixtures, etc.? 


Toronto, Canada, June, 1954 


33 



Personnel 

Yes No 


Are your floating drums free from leaks and your supporting dock 
logs sound and buoyant ? 

Have you set up a defence against swimmers moving under the 
docks and becoming lost or entangled in “under dock construc¬ 
tion” ? 

Have you thoroughly examined and measured your one approved 
diving area to make certain that under your 1 metre board 
there is a minimum of nine feet of water, and under your 3 
metre board there is at least twelve feet? 

Have you similarly checked your beginner area for a- depth of 
3 to 3/2 feet, your intermediate area for a depth of 3j/ 2 to 
7 feet, and your senior area over 7 feet? 

and Programme 

Has your waterfront director professional rating? Has your water¬ 
front director Red Cross and Royal Life Saving Society or 
Y.M.C.A. qualifications? 

Is he absolutely conscientious and responsible? 

Has he personality as a teacher? 

Has he a thorough and practical knowledge of camping as well as 
waterfront activity? 

Has he confidence and does he display some sense of loyalty to you 
and the camp? 

Have you tried to select other staff members who are qualified to 
serve on the waterfront as responsible assistants? 

Have you provided the waterfront director with a reasonably ac¬ 
curate summary of the age and number of campers ? 

Have you given him a summary of the equipment on hand or what 
equipment has been purchased? 

Have you outlined clearly to the waterfront director what you 
expect of him; i.e., checking patrols, equipment, progress of 
swimmers, awards, etc., judgment in case of bad weather, etc. ? 

Have you established with your waterfront director and all other 
staff members a set of rules and regulations which can be 
consistently adhered to through all phases of the camp session? 

Is your checking system thoroughly satisfactory, or should you 
ask for help in its revision? 

Are you providing your waterfront director with time and oppor¬ 
tunity to train the staff (particularly waterfront assistants), 
in methods of instruction, technique of teaching, water safety, 
artificial respiration, etc.? 

Are you making plans well ahead of time for major events, such 
as regattas, aquacades, etc.? 

For these events have you selected items which are not unduly 
hazardous to participants? 

Have you selected events within the capacity of participants? 

Can all items within your special events be readily supervised? 

Can you be consistent in your waterfront rules and regulations in 
your plan for special events? 

Have you arranged for a pre-camp training session in which you 
and your waterfront director can discuss plans for the summer s 
waterfront activity with other members of the staff? 


34 


Canadian Camping 


Are you making provision ior instruction ol all levels of campers; 
non-swimmers or beginners, intermediates and seniors? 

Are you allowing for instruction of “special cases” that have been 
accepted into your camp? 

Have you made allowance on application forms for a specific 
appraisal of campers’ swimming ability? 

Have you arranged for an “entry to camp” swim test in which the 
waterfront director can group campers into ability levels and 
also re-allocate swimmers who tend to exaggerate ability on 
application forms? 

Equipment 

Yes No Have you checked your docks for broken boards? 

Have you considered the necessity for another coat of paint? 

If you use “cocoa matting” is it still in good condition? 

Have your diving boards any longitudinal cracks? 

Have you checked your waterfront area for excessively slippery 
areas? (use sand on fresh paint). 

Have you considered an extra diving board to be changed periodi¬ 
cally with your regular one? 

Are your float lines and floats in good condition? (for float lines 
use hot mixture of paraffin and kerosene). 

Are your ladders solid? 

Is your enclosed entrance to the waterfront still sound and satis¬ 
factory in appearance?

Arc your ring buoys buoyant and in good repair? 

Are your reaching aids (preferably bamboo poles) adequate in 
number and dependable in structure? 

Are your notice boards striking in appearance and still well located. 
Have you recently checked your waterfront first aid kits? 

Have you acquired necessary accessory equipment for your special 
events? 

Have you the following small items of equipment for the watertront: 
megaphones and whistles 
stop watch 

starting gun or clapper 
water polo balls or water balls 
hooks, and oilcloth cover for bulletin board 
specimen copies of certificates, emblems and pins for which

Is your life saving equipment within reach and in good repair. 

i.e. paddleboards, striped boat blankets, reaching aids, etc.? 

Is your waterfront set up so that swimmers at all levels cannot 
become entangled in chains, wires, etc., used in anchorage? 

Health and Safety 

Yes No Have you made arrangements to check water temperatures through¬ 
out the camp season? 

Have you arranged for regular pollution checks of your water, 
through the Department of Health? 

Do your waterfront director, and staff assistants, understand 
that individual resistance to water temperatures vary a great 
deal as do psychological attitudes toward swimming? 

Have vou arranged to have a regular check for infectious skin 
abrasions and cuts, athlete’s foot, etc., before entering the 

swimming area? , . , , 

Have you racks outside or adjacent to the swim area for such 
personal items as towels, extra clothing, shoes, etc 
Do you permit swimming outside swim areas? (you should not). 
Do you permit swimming at dock or at night? (you should not). 
Do you permit only qualified persons to use row boats, canoes, 

sailboats? ... , » . ■> 

Do you keep campers off docks unless qualified persons are on duty? 

Do you permit horseplay on docks? (you should not). 

Do you have some kind of preparatory exercises before entering the 

water ? 

Do you guard against excessive sun exposure on waterfront?

Canadian Camping 



Now, if you have scored poorly on this check list, you have some very 
important and worthwhile improvements to make in your camp. This should 
be interesting and challenging to your staff and camp board or committee. 
If you are sure you have scored well make very certain that everything is kept 
that way and that you maintain a high standard in your waterfront for 
children to have a safe, happy and educational experience! 

For detailed information on any phase of waterfront programme, con¬ 
struction and planning, etc., please consult the following persons. 7'hcy will 
be delighted to assist you in developing a finer waterfront: 

1. Mr. W. F. Glayson, Director, Swimming and Water Safety, 

Canadian Red Gross Society, Ontario Division, 460 Jarvis St., Toronto 5. 

2. Mr. L. B. Smith, Executive Officer, Physical Education Branch, 

Department of Education, 206 Huron Street, Toronto 5. 

3. Mrs. J. M. Pretty, 206 St. Leonard’s Avenue, Toronto 12

THE CAMP PROGRAMME BOOK. 

Catherine T. Hammett and Virginia 

Musselman. 

There’s no better way for campers 
and counsellors to get to know one 
another than through working together 
on camp programme. This book, which 
some readers may already know, is a 
one-volume encyclopedia on everything 
that goes into camp life as it relates 
to the camper . . . programme plan¬ 
ning, living in the out-doors, related 
programme activities, composite activi¬ 
ties, specific plans for programmes, how 
to carry them out, how to hold the 
interest of campers. 

“Theory, however, is not enough,” 
the authors tell us. “It is the aim of 
this book to go farther, to show theory 
put to work, by describing not just 
what happens in camp, but how it 
happens and why. It is based on the 
philosophy that camping is learning 
to live together, learning to know and 
to enjoy doing things in camp that 
cannot be done in town.” $6.00. An 
Association Press book, distributed in 
Canada through G. R. Welch Com¬ 
pany, Limited, Toronto.

is able to set down those essentials to

Canadian Camping 









Propane Gas 


for Camp Cooking 


% 


> 




When camp operators consider pro¬ 
pane gas for use in their camps, one 
of the first questions they ask is, “Is 
it safe?” This question was answered 
with authority by Division Chief C. L. 
Blickstead, of the Montreal Fire 
Department Training School, who said 
in an article which appeared recently 
in the Oil and Gas Heat magazine, 
“LP Gas is no more dangerous than 
water when properly handled and 
when proper equipment is used.” 

Unlike manufactured and natural 
gas, propane is non-poisonous. Its 
unvarying chemical formula, CeH8, 
provides a 1 pure fuel with a constant 
heat content. Reputable propane gas 
distributors ensure safety in the use 
of propane by following regulations 
laid down by the Dominion Board of 
Insurance Underwriters. When con¬ 
sidering the installation of propane 
equipment at your camp, make sure 
your distributor follows DBIU pam¬ 
phlet 58, the propane man’s “Bible”. 
The regulations contained in Pamphlet 
58 were inherited from the National 
Fire Protection Association and are the 
result of long experience in the pro¬ 
pane industry throughout the United 
States. Adherence to these regulations 
has produced an enviable safety repu¬ 
tation. Reliable propane dealers will 
use and sell only containers and equip¬ 
ment approved by the Interstate Com¬ 
merce Commission or its Canadian 
counterpart, the Board of Transport 
Commissioners for Canada. 

Propane itself is odourless but, as a 
protection in the detection of leaks, an 
odourant is added to propane which 


makes its presence .known as quickly 
as a frightened skunk. Approved pro¬ 
pane appliances are equipped with 
safety shut-off valves which prevent 
unburned fuel from escaping into the 
open air if pilots are accidently blown 
out. If your appliances refuse to light, 
therefore, you know you must check 
the equipment before re-lighting ovens 
or water heater burners. 

When you close up camp for the 
winter, the fuel should be shut off at 
the cylinders. Propane left standing in 
the cylinders during the winter will be 
ready to go to work when camp is 
opened up in the spring. 

A network of agents and dealers 
throughout most of Canada make pro¬ 
pane gas readily available for camps. 
If you are on a road, your dealer may 
deliver right to your camp and hook 
up cylinders to your installation, or if 
you are some distance from a road and 
accessible only by water, your dis¬ 
tributor may deliver to the nearest 
point he can reach with his truck and 
leave it up to the camp operator to 
transport from the dock to the camp. 
One distributor in the Georgian Bay 
area delivers cylinders by air! 

Cylinders should always be trans¬ 
ported standing upright with the 
cylinder caps on and, as an added pre¬ 
caution, as far as possible from the 
motor of a boat. For example, if the 
boat has an outboard motor, the 
cylinders should ride in the bow, or can 
be towed in a smaller craft behind. 
People accustomed to handling drums 
of gasoline or fuel oil will find that

moving a 100 lb. cylinder of propane 
is child’s play in comparison. Your 
propane distributor can show you the 
easy way to handle cylinders. 

An installation to serve cooking and 
water heating appliances consists of a 
number of 100 lb. cylinders. Cylinders 
are generally hooked up in series with 
an equal number on each side of the 
regulating equipment. For example, a 
four cylinder hook-up will have two 
cylinders on each side of the regulating 
equipment with the fuel flowing sim¬ 
ultaneously from the two cylinders on 
one side. When these are empty, the 
automatic change-over manifold will 
transfer the source of supply to the 
two full cylinders. 

The number of cylinders required is 
determined by the peak load, that is, 
the maximum amount of gas required 
at any given moment. An experienced 
propane man will estimate accurately 
your peak load and suggest the proper 
number of cylinders. If he says you 
need a battery of sixteen cylinders, it 
may seem a lot to you, but unless you 
accept his advice you may find your 
cook struggling to prepare a meal with 
insufficient pressure to run all the burn¬ 
ers on the stove at the same time. 
Remember, the distributor’s aim is to 
create another satisfied propane user. 

The fuel is transferred from the 
cylinders to the appliances through 
copper tubing or, in the case of very 
large batteries of ranges, through rigid 
pipe. Again your propane distributor’s 
experience guides the choice of pipe 
or tubing, to ensure proper pressure at 
the appliances. 

The installation charge in the Mus- 
koka and Algonquin Park area, for 
example, is $46.75 plus $3.25 for each 
additional cylinder over two. Propane 
gas is generally sold on a sliding scale 



42 


Canadian Camping 





of rates, with the price per cylinder 
becoming progressively lower as con¬ 
sumption increases. The cost of using 
propane for cooking is dependent on 
many individual factors, such as re¬ 
moteness from supply, type of equip¬ 
ment used, or the way in which the 
cook uses the equipment. It is an old 
saying that the gas company makes its 
profit on the fuel wasted by the cook. 
A hypothetical camp with 100 people, 
including the staff, will be able to cook 
meals and do home baking for only lc 
a person per meal. Considering that 
the camp has its full complement of 
100 for 66 days, the fuel cost at an 
average cylinder price of $9.00 will be 
just under $200.00. If the camp uses 
propane for water heating as well as 
cooking, the per cylinder price will 
come down and the cooking costs will 
also be reduced. A larger camp, too, 
will have the advantage of a lower 
gas rate. Propane gas comes into its 
full usefullness when put to additional 
work heating water, drying clothes and 
incinerating garbage, all automatically. 
When the price of propane is balanced 
against the savings in time and labour, 
additional efficiency, better working 
conditions and the advantages of better 
cooked, tastier meals, propane is in¬ 
expensive indeed. 

Propane gas can also be used effi¬ 
ciently for automatic heating of small 
areas. When sold in cylinders, it is not 
practical to consider heating a whole 
house or large building with propane, 
particularly in the winter months, but 
for chilly spring and fall evenings, a 
propane gas space heater will give 
efficient and automatic heat in cottages 
and cabins.

LITTLE CANADA 
IN ENGLAND 

All of us in Canada have a deep 
interest in Tonakela, “Wally” Forgie’s 
camp just outside Madras, India. We 
keep abreast of the times in following 
camping trends in other parts of the 
world . . . Finland, Germany, the 

United States, Australia, Scotland, even 
in places as remote as Japan. 

But within the last six weeks comes 
an envoy from England whose life-hope 
it is to build a Canadian camp in 
Surrey, this to operate twelve months 
in the year as a place of learning and 
recuperation for sickly children from 
all parts of Mr. Churchill’s Little 
Island. 

Lt.-Commander Frank Hunt of 
the Royal Navy, member of Sir Winston 
Churchill’s Map Room Staff during the 
War, and designer of his famous 
“Dunkirk to Berlin” Map, has been a 
frequent and welcome visitor to your 
National Office, where he has talked 
with members about logs and log cabins, 
designs and costs, people to visit, 
counsellors and programme, and the 
link the Canadian Camping Association 
will eventually have with Little Canada 
in England. At the moment we stand 
about a quarter of a century ahead 
of ourselves! But why not take the 
long view? 

Commander Hunt’s interest and 
hobby has always been the welfare 
of small children. As he has said, “I 
turned to this sort of work rather than 
to golf for relaxation”, and he found 
that in England there is little or no 
provision made for the six- to twelve- 
year-old child who is sickly but not ill 
enough to be sent to hospital 

Sir Winston Churchill gave his bless¬ 
ing to the venture, and the late King 

(continued page 47)

George VI, whose love for camping 
was so widely known, was keenly in¬ 
terested in its development. Our own 
Governor General has known of the 
project since its very beginning and 
a host of Canadians who are influential 
in the professional and business world 
are now taking an active interest. 

The trick is to get the logs. With the 
dollar situation and stiff import regula¬ 
tions, there are problems. So Com¬ 
mander Hunt is here to interest lumber 
tycoons in each province to lend a 
hand by supplying logs and shipping 
them over for the purpose. It is now 
our hope that as he travels across 
Canada, he will be in touch as well, 
with camping people in each province, 
so that in some way we can tie in with 


Little Canada later on when the camp 
is in operation. Cabins, by the way, are 
to be named after each province and 
after cities in Canada. 

So, during the next few months, as 
Commander Hunt travels out to the 
West Coast and back again, you will 
hear about him and see him, and 
welcome him as a guest at your camps 
possibly, for he would like to see as 
many as he has time to see, while they 
are in operation. 

With him goes our blessing on the 
venture, and a hope that in some way 
our association with this new and 
worthy field of endeavour will be as 
strong as it is with Tonakela.
