Counselor on the fiob 

R. D. “Dick” McDonald, 

Chairman , OCA Training Courses . 


“Hey! You heard what I told you. 
Jim!” 

Tom had yelled this way often 
enough during the summer for the 
Camp Director to have realized that 
he was really throwing out an S.O.S. 
because this character in his cabin had 
him beaten. However, the camp coun¬ 
sellors had all had a long training 
course through the winter, and for the 
week before camp opening. Tom’s cry 
for help was not heard because nobody 
really thought of him as a person need¬ 
ing help. He had been a counsellor-in¬ 
training for one year, and this was his 
second year as a full counsellor. He 
had been a good camper, with plenty 
of skills, and was generally liked by 
everyone in the camp. 

There are many “Toms” at camp 
because some directors do not see the 
camp period itself as the most import¬ 
ant one for genuine training. 

The counsellor can learn many skills 
at many points during the year. Life¬ 
saving, crafts, archery and scores of 
other “activity” skills do not require 
the camp setting and the camp experi¬ 
ence for the counsellor to acquire a 
good learning experience. 

But almost the only setting available 
to the camp management adequate for 
training the counsellor for his real job 
of being a “counsellor” in the field of 
human relations is the camp in session. 
Obviously, at camp, and only at camp, 
does the camp director have the 
counsellor in a position where he has 
to accept responsibility for his actions. 
Not even the period of camp before the 
campers arrive is of much value for 


“counsellor” training in the true sense 
of the word. The counsellor is still free 
of responsibility for his group. 

A counsellor training programme 
should include such content as “Under¬ 
standing the Camper”, “The Philos¬ 
ophy of Camping”, “Understanding 
Group Life”, “The Meaning of Dis¬ 
cipline” and similar subjects. However, 
the key to counsellor training is actually 
helping him, like the Greeks, to under¬ 
stand himself. The counsellor is no 
counsellor at all until he understands 
the relationship between what he does 
and what the other members in his 
group do individually and collectively. 
And if it is a part of Canadian camp¬ 
ing to teach democracy, then the 
counsellor is not performing his duty 
unless his conscious efforts are assisting 
his campers and himself to include 
every member in the decision-making 
that takes place all day long. 

It is probably true to say that the 
average counsellor becomes more auto¬ 
cratic as the camp season wears on 
. . . unless he is helped at times when 
he is having genuine difficulty in 
understanding himself, his campers, and 
his group. The actual experience he is 
having and his relationship to it be¬ 
come a learning opportunity because 
he is responsible for the outcome. 

The usual behaviour when a difficult 
situation arises and there is failure to 
understand what is involved, is for the 
counsellor to “take over” in order to 
keep control of it. This type of solution 
of a problem tends to occur more 
frequently through time as the counsel¬ 
lor becomes increasingly tired and. 


48 


Canadian Camping 


therefore, less willing to think and feel 
a problem through. His very tenseness 
makes observation of himself and the 
situation improbable. 

Lack of an in-camp, experience- 
centred training programme affects a 
counsellor in this way because he 
arrives at camp with attitudes that 
make the authoritarian way out of his 
difficulties very easy. Some of these 
are: “The campers are too young to 
make good decisions”; “I am in charge, 
and have a right to lay down the law”; 
“If I make the campers do the right 
things, they are learning what is good 
for them”; “Campers should look to 
their leader”; “So what if they do it 
because they like me?” 

So that an in-camp training pro¬ 
gramme will help free a counsellor of 
these decision-prohibiting attitudes, the 
following dynamics are needed in the 
experience: 

1. The counsellor must be provided 
with a personal experience as a mem¬ 
ber of a democratic training group. 

2. The material must be subjective, 
making the counsellor aware of him¬ 
self. 

3. He should share his growing 
experience with others in the same 
programme. High morale in the train¬ 
ing group provides a stimulating 
climate in which learning can take 
place. 

4. The training method constantly 
should get the counsellor to establish 
principles by which his actions may be 
evaluated. 

5. The counsellor should be pro¬ 
vided with a friendly atmosphere where 
self-criticism can be helpful. 

6. The training programme should 
help the counsellor to work with the 
specific problem he has at the time 
when he has it. There is nothing like 
a few productive experiences to make 
the counsellor take the next steps in 
his growth to maturity and self-realiza¬ 
tion.

Mr. John Hoyle paM high tribute 
to Mr. Yard’s term of bffic’e as Presi¬ 
dent of the National Association. He 
cited him as a man who “gets things 
done”, and credited him with the union 
of the provincial associations as they 
stand today, and with the organization 
of the Alberta association, both 
through much personal effort and time. 
Mr. Hoyle voiced the feeling of the 
meeting when he said that he hoped 
Mr. Yard would now devote his talents 
to one of the committees. 

Our arrival in Kingston was hailed 
with a greatly appreciated tour of the 
city, arranged by Miss Cleta Herman 
and Miss Isobel Lyon of Kingston 
YWCA, and a trip to their Camp 
Cedarnook. It closed with a dinner at 
the LaSalle Hotel, during which we 
continued to “talk shop”, speaking of 
plans which may sound far-fetched at 
the present time, but which will surely 
come to pass before too many years 
have gone by.
